claims.text: A homogeneous distribution of multiple principal elements induces uniform lattice distortions in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Uniform lattice distortions reduce atomic mobility through sluggish diffusion.
Reduced atomic mobility suppresses phase segregation.
Sluggish diffusion and suppressed phase segregation improve structural and chemical stability at high temperatures.
The relevant initial material is a single-phase high-entropy nanoalloy with a homogeneous multielement distribution.
An inert or vacuum environment minimizes oxidation and other external chemical influences during thermal treatment.
High configurational entropy produces uniform lattice distortion.
Uniform lattice distortion maintains a consistent local chemical environment.
Uniform lattice distortion impedes atomic rearrangements.
Lattice distortion creates energetic barriers that slow atomic diffusion.
Slower diffusion inhibits environmental reactions such as oxidation relative to less compositionally complex alloys.
Compared with a binary or ternary nanoalloy baseline, a high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit lower diffusion rates during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Compared with the baseline, a high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit less phase separation during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Compared with the baseline, a high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit lower oxidation or degradation rates.
Binary or ternary nanoalloys lack the high configurational entropy of alloys containing five or more principal elements.
The prediction is limited to nanoalloys with an initially uniform elemental distribution.
The prediction excludes exposures involving extreme thermal gradients or rapid oxidation in reactive atmospheres.
Interfacial energy and external conditions may also affect high-temperature stability.
